titulo: Análise histológica da miotoxicidade do veneno de Micrurus spixii (cobra coral amazônica) em músculo biventer cervicis de pintainho e sua neutralização por soro antielapídico
titulo_curto: Amazonian coral snake venom in muscle, and how much the antivenom protects

em_1_minuto.titulo: A venom that attacks nerves and muscles
em_1_minuto.texto: Snakebites are a neglected tropical disease. The Amazonian coral snake (Micrurus spixii) has a venom that paralyzes and also damages muscle.

em_1_minuto.titulo: Venom, with and without antivenom, under the microscope
em_1_minuto.texto: Chick muscles were exposed to the venom, alone or pre-mixed with the antivenom used in Brazil, and the damaged cells were counted under the microscope.
With the venom, healthy cells dropped from 66% to less than 1%. With the antivenom, they rose to about 5%.
The antivenom protected well against swelling and cell death, but little against other damage. It is made with the venom of two other coral snake species.

secoes.titulo: The Amazonian coral snake and its venom
secoes.lede: Coral snakes are secretive and produce little venom, but a bite is always treated as serious.

blocos.html: There are about 80 species of coral snakes of the genus Micrurus in the Americas; in Brazil, 38 have been recorded. Micrurus spixii, the Amazonian coral snake, lives in the Brazilian states of Acre, Amazonas, Mato Grosso, Pará and Rondônia. These snakes hide in damp, dark places, often buried, and produce little venom.

blocos.titulo: The two toxin families in the venom

itens.texto: They block the receptors that receive the nerve signal in muscle. They are the main cause of paralysis.
Enzymes that “digest” cell membranes. Besides acting on nerves, they damage muscle: this is myotoxicity.

blocos.html: In Brazil, the treatment is the bivalent antielapidic serum, produced in horses with the venom of two other coral snakes (M. frontalis and M. corallinus). The Ministry of Health recommends 10 vials intravenously and considers every coral snake bite potentially serious, because of the risk of respiratory failure.
Venom varies a lot from one species to another. So it was not known whether this antivenom protects against the muscle damage caused by the Amazonian coral snake. That is the study's question.

secoes.lede: A lab experiment with three groups of muscles, analyzed blindly under the microscope.

itens.texto: Chick biventer cervicis muscles (3 per group) spent 2 hours in Krebs nutrient solution (control), with M. spixii venom (10 µg/mL) or with venom pre-mixed with the antivenom.
Before touching the muscle, the venom spent 30 minutes at 37 °C with 0.03 mL of antielapidic serum, in the proportion recommended by the manufacturer.
The muscles were fixed in formalin, embedded in paraffin and cut into 4 µm slices, stained with hematoxylin-eosin.
The slides were analyzed double-blind at 400× magnification, counting healthy cells and those with each type of damage.
Mean ± standard error, compared by ANOVA and Tukey's test. A difference counts as significant when p < 0.05.

blocos.html: The 10 µg/mL dose came from an earlier study by the group: 5 µg/mL caused little damage and 20 µg/mL caused too much to measure the antivenom's effect. The protocol was approved by Uniso's Animal Use Ethics Committee (no. 229/2022).

secoes.titulo: How to recognize each type of damage
secoes.lede: With hematoxylin-eosin staining, muscle fibers appear pink. Each type of damage leaves a different mark.

blocos.alt: Pink-stained muscle section, with arrows pointing to normal cells, edema, vacuoles, myofibril condensation and ghost cells
blocos.legenda: Figure 1 · Types of damage in chick biventer cervicis muscle (hematoxylin-eosin; bar = 40 µm).

itens.texto: Intact fiber with a regular shape.
The cell swells as fluid builds up. It is usually one of the first signs of damage.
Empty spaces inside the cell, a sign of a damaged membrane.
The fibers that make muscle contract clump into dark areas and lose their organization.
The fiber dies (myonecrosis), leaving an almost empty space with loose nuclei.

secoes.titulo: What the venom did, and what the antivenom prevented
secoes.lede: Choose a cell type to compare the three groups.

parametros.leitura: The venom wiped out almost all the healthy cells. When pre-mixed with the antivenom, it preserved about 5 times more cells (4.8% versus 0.92%), still far below the control.
The venom slightly increased cell swelling. With the antivenom, edema fell even below the control: it was the best-neutralized damage.
The venom doubled the cells with vacuoles. The antivenom reduced this damage by about 13%.
With the venom, 72% of the cells had condensed fibers, versus 54% in the control. The antivenom reduced this damage by about 13%.
Dead cells appeared only with the venom. The antivenom almost abolished this damage: with it, the result was no different from the control.

blocos.nota: Mean ± standard error (3 muscles per group). * different from control; # different from venom (p < 0.05). A cell may have more than one type of damage, so the percentages don't add up to 100%. The control group had some storage and handling artifacts, which explains part of its damage.

itens.legenda: Figure 2 · Quantitative analysis of the damage: (a) normal cells, (b) edema, (c) vacuoles, (d) condensed myofibrils, (e) ghost cells.
Figure 1 · Classification of the types of cell damage (hematoxylin-eosin; bar = 40 µm).

secoes.lede: The damage follows a chain of events, and the antivenom works best at its start.

itens: Calcium floods into the cell uncontrolled

blocos.html:
The venom's PLA2 enzymes rupture the muscle fiber membrane. Calcium floods in uncontrolled, vacuoles appear and the myofibrils condense, until the fiber dies. Edema is one of the first steps in this chain: by reducing it, the antivenom also prevented the final stage, the ghost cells.

Why was the protection only partial? The antivenom used in Brazil is made with the venom of just two species, and its ability to neutralize the venom of other coral snakes varies. Earlier studies had already shown that the Amazonian coral snake's venom is among the most lethal in the genus and that this antivenom does not fully neutralize its phospholipase activity.
In earlier tests with mice, the same antivenom offered little protection against this venom's muscle damage, even at twice the recommended dose.

The Amazonian coral snake's venom causes myonecrosis in muscle, and the antielapidic serum, pre-mixed with the venom, gave significant protection, but to different degrees for each type of damage. The authors attribute the damage mainly to PLA2; the role of 3FTx and other toxins still needs to be studied.

itens: Lab (in vitro) study, using chick muscle.
Only one antivenom-to-venom ratio was tested.
The control group had some slide-preparation artifacts.

glossario.def: A substance's ability to damage muscle.
Ability to damage or block the nervous system; in coral snakes, it causes paralysis.
A bird neck muscle widely used in the lab to study how venoms act on nerves and muscles.
Antivenom against coral snakes, produced in horses. In Brazil it is made with the venom of M. frontalis and M. corallinus.
Venom enzyme that breaks down the lipids in cell membranes.
Three-finger toxins, which block the nerve-signal receptors in muscle.
Classic slide stain: it turns nuclei purple and cytoplasm pink.
Analysis in which the evaluator doesn't know which group each sample belongs to, to avoid bias.
Mixing the venom with the antivenom and waiting a while before applying it to the muscle.
Experiment done outside the living organism, in the lab.
Statistical criterion: the difference is considered real, not due to chance, with less than a 5% chance of error.
